title: Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ada

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states 'ALFAR employs light training to optimize its fusion weights and attention reallocation parameters, which involve fine-tuning on selected benchmarks, thereby limiting its plug-and-play capability' and immediately after says 'As a plug-and-play method, ALFAR achieves superior performance ... without requiring additional training or external tools'. These two claims directly contradict each other, and the rest of the paper describes ALFAR as training-free, with no fine-tuning step.

The paper title reads 'Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ada' but the method introduced is ALFAR (Adaptive Logits Fusion and Attention Reallocation). The title is truncated and does not match the method name used throughout the paper.

The text claims 'We address the attention preference ... by adaptively adjusting model attention ... based on the retrieval similarity α ... Specifically, less attention is allocated to image tokens if the context is more reliable with a high retrieval similarity.' However, the only attention adjustment formula presented (Eq. 7) uses a query-context relevance score ω_j and does not incorporate the retrieval similarity α. There is no equation that reduces attention to image tokens based on α, making the method description inconsistent with the presented equations.

Eq. (11) defines the fused logits as softmax(λ_v^t · logit_p + λ_c^t · logit_c). The text states 'ensuring positive weights that sum to 1' but λ_v^t and λ_c^t are defined in Eq. (10) as sums of attention weights over image and context tokens. Since the attention distribution over all tokens sums to 1, λ_v^t + λ_c^t is generally less than 1 (the remaining attention goes to query and generated tokens). The description that the two weights sum to 1 contradicts the definitions unless an unstated normalization is applied.

The text says 'scalability issues emerge with larger models, as demonstrated by the performance decline on InstructBLIP 13B in Tab. 8 and Fig. 6.' Fig. 6 shows a qualitative example of generated responses and attention distributions for LLaVA-1.5, not any information about performance decline or scalability of larger models. The figure is incorrectly cited as evidence for that claim.

The reported standard deviations for ALFAR on InstructBLIP across all Human and Validation splits are exactly ±0.00 (e.g., 5.98±0.00, 5.67±0.00, 4.55±0.00, 5.68±0.00). The paper states multinomial sampling is used and that results are averaged over three runs. Obtaining exactly the same accuracy in three independent runs with multinomial sampling is highly improbable, raising suspicion that the runs were not truly independent or that the standard deviations are fabricated/rounded inaccurately.
